The literal rule (also called the literal interpretation) is a method of interpretation of a written law that looks to the precise wording of the provision and ignores any effect which may not be intended by the drafters but which arises out of the words used. The Golden Rule is the first principle of statutory interpretation which states that courts must interpret legislation in a way that avoids absurd or irrational outcomes. The mischief rule is a fundamental principle of statutory interpretation that requires courts to interpret legislation in a manner that addresses the mischief, harm or defect that the legislature intended to remedy. The natural rule is a term sometimes used in place of the literal rule. It refers to the idea that when interpreting legislation, the court should look at what the plain language of the text says without adding anything from other sources. The Common Rule is a legal doctrine that holds that where there are two inconsistent provisions in an Act, the later provision will prevail over the earlier one unless it is clear that both were intended to apply concurrently.
